content: 1. The volume of items to be incinerated is expected to be substantial; therefore, the design of burning pits must accommodate this capacity effectively. 2. Items that are unsuitable for incineration should be buried deeply at an approved site to ensure safe disposal. 3. Before disposal, all items must undergo thorough decontamination to eliminate potential risks to health workers and contamination of water sources. 4. Once burning pits are no longer in use, they should be sealed with a one-meter layer of soil to ensure proper closure. 5. The coordinates of all final waste disposal sites must be recorded and logged with the Ministry of Health (MoH) for future reference. 6. Incinerator drums should be emptied into waste pits and, if reusable, sterilized by igniting a fuel source (e.g., kerosene) and allowing them to burn for 10–15 minutes. 7. Sharps pits and organic pits should be backfilled, compacted, and covered with a minimum of 5 cm of concrete for permanent closure. 8. Ash pits pose limited risk; they should be backfilled with soil, compacted, and clearly marked for future reference. Decontamination of Medical Devices and Equipment 9. Cleaning, disinfection, and sterilization procedures for medical devices vary depending on the type and complexity of the equipment. 10. Decontamination standard operating procedures (SOPs) provided by manufacturers should be followed whenever available. 11. In the absence of manufacturer-specific instructions, generic SOPs outlined in Annex 3 should be adhered to. 12. Risks associated with reusing medical devices include disease transmission, inadequate device performance after reprocessing, and occupational exposure to infectious materials. 13. Medical devices should be categorized based on their design and complexity to determine appropriate decontamination methods. Categories of Medical Assets 14. Medical furniture, such as beds, tables, and utensils, requires individual screening before decontamination procedures are specified. 15. Non-electro-mechanical hospital equipment, such as tourniquets and measuring tapes, should be cleaned and disinfected according to SOP 1. 16. Electro-mechanical hospital equipment, including lamps, thermometers, and defibrillators, should be dismantled, cleaned, and disinfected as per SOP 2. 17. Respiratory equipment, such as oxygen concentrators and ventilators, should be disassembled, cleaned, and disinfected following SOP 3. 18. Single-use devices, such as syringes and catheters, should be disposed of immediately in clearly labeled, puncture-resistant containers. Planning for Decontamination 19. Conduct an inventory of medical assets using WHO guidance and categorize them based on their characteristics. 20. Allocate designated spaces for contaminated items and decontamination activities, ensuring separation from cleaned items. 21. Use appropriate cleaning agents and disinfectants, such as 5% chlorine solution or 70% ethanol, ensuring compatibility with manufacturer instructions. 22. Ensure consumables like plastic bags are available to protect cleaned equipment from recontamination. Waste Management 23. Hazardous materials, such as plastics and irreparable medical devices, should be deeply buried or transported offsite for safe disposal. 24. Expired medications should be disposed of according to WHO or national guidelines, while non-expired, unopened medications may be redirected to other facilities if stored under proper conditions. Laboratory Equipment Decontamination 25. Laboratory equipment should be decontaminated using methods such as steam autoclaving or immersion in 70% ethanol for at least 10 minutes. 26. Biosafety cabinets (BSCs) require proper fumigation and decontamination by qualified personnel before decommissioning. 27. Automated analyzers used for Ebola testing should be decontaminated as per manufacturer recommendations, with special attention to biohazardous waste. Occupational Health and Safety 28. Workers involved in decommissioning must follow strict procedures to minimize risks of infection and other occupational hazards. 29. Full personal protective equipment (PPE) should be worn in high-risk zones, while lower-level PPE may be used in low-risk zones. 30. Trained and supervised personnel should handle contaminated items and ensure proper cleaning and decontamination processes. 31. Measures to prevent and control risks, including biological, chemical, and psychosocial hazards, should be planned and implemented in accordance with national health standards.
